propositions.text: The Appellant is a Pakistani citizen claiming refugee protection as a Shia Muslim married to a Sunni, fearing family disapproval and threats.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Pakistan, claims that she is a Convention refugee and/or a person in need of protection. She claims that, as she is a Shia Muslim and has married a man of the Sunni Muslim faith, her family's disapproval of the marriage threatens her safety. Further, her husband's ex-wife has threatened her.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant, a Pakistani Shia Muslim married to a Sunni, claims refugee protection due to family disapproval and threats, including from husband's ex-wife.

propositions.text: The RPD rejected the Appellant's refugee claim on June 21, 2018.
propositions.quote: She has appealed a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated June 21, 2018, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.

propositions.text: There is insufficient credible evidence to support the Appellant's claim and an internal flight alternative exists in Islamabad.
propositions.quote: Having reviewed the record, I find that there is insufficient credible evidence to support her claim. Further, in the alternative, she has an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Islamabad.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the claim; the court finds insufficient evidence and an internal flight alternative, dismissing the appeal.

propositions.text: The Appellant bases her claim on certain grounds.
propositions.quote: The Appellant bases her claim on the following:

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant bases her claim on specified grounds.

propositions.text: The Appellant is Shia, refused arranged marriage, married a Sunni in 2008, and fears her brother's threats due to family dishonour.
propositions.quote: The Appellant follows the Shia faith. Her family had arranged for her to be married to a cousin. Instead, she married her husband in April 2008. Her family did not approve. Specifically, her brother, who belongs to a gang, threatened her. She fears her brother who wants to take vengeance for dishonouring the family by refusing to comply with the arranged marriage and marry another who is a Sunni.

propositions.text: She fears her husband's ex-wife and family who attacked her in 2016 for being Shia; police dismissed her report.
propositions.quote: She also fears her husband's ex-wife and her family who attacked her in 2016 for being a Shia. She reported the attack to the police who dismissed her.

propositions.text: She left Pakistan in 2017, came to Canada, and claimed protection.
propositions.quote: She left Pakistan in XXXX 2017. She came to Canada and claimed protection.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant, a Shia, refused arranged marriage, fears threats from brother and husband's ex-wife's family, left Pakistan in 2017, and claimed protection in Canada.

propositions.text: The RPD held a hearing on June 21, 2018, and rejected the Appellant's claim.
propositions.quote: The RPD held a hearing on June 21, 2018 and gave the bench decision on that date. It found that the Appellant's claim did not have sufficient credible evidence.

propositions.text: The Appellant appealed the RPD decision to the RAD.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has appealed to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).

paragraphs.summary: The RPD held a hearing and rejected the claim; the Appellant appealed to the RAD.

propositions.text: There is insufficient credible evidence that the Appellant is a Convention refugee or person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: Having reviewed the record, I find that there is insufficient credible evidence that the Appellant is a Convention refugee and/or a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds insufficient credible evidence that the Appellant qualifies as a refugee or person in need of protection.

propositions.text: After August 20, 2018, the Appellant submitted four new pieces of evidence: two affidavits, a medical report, and a pharmacy prescription.
propositions.quote: After the appeal was perfected on August 20, 2018, the Appellant submitted four pieces of evidence onto the record. These include: * an affidavit from the Appellant's spouse; * an affidavit from the Appellant's friend; * a medical report from the XXXX XXXX, dated August 11, 2018; and * a prescription from a pharmacy in Canada dated August 10, 2018.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submitted four new evidentiary documents after August 20, 2018.

propositions.text: The Appellant's statement that she had no new evidence and did not seek a hearing is confusing, but the new evidence is considered admissible.
propositions.quote: In the Written Statement in the Appeal Record, the Appellant wrote in her statement that she did not have new evidence and did not seek a hearing. This is somewhat confusing. However, I have considered whether the new evidence is admissible and found that it is for the following reasons.

paragraphs.summary: Despite contradictory statements, the court finds the new evidence admissible.

propositions.text: The new evidence post-dates the rejection and was not reasonably available before; it is allowed onto the record.
propositions.quote: All of the evidence post-dates the date of rejection. I find that it was not reasonably available beforehand. I allow the evidence onto the record.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the new evidence onto the record as it was not reasonably available before rejection.

propositions.text: The Appellant requested an oral hearing in new submissions despite earlier stating she did not.
propositions.quote: Similarly, the Appellant has requested an oral hearing in her new submissions, although she wrote in her Written Statement that she did not request one.

propositions.text: The RAD will not hold an oral hearing for specified reasons.
propositions.quote: The RAD will not hold a hearing for the following reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant inconsistently requested an oral hearing; the RAD decides not to hold one.

propositions.text: Subsection 110(6) of the Act permits RAD hearings only when new evidence raises serious credibility issues, is central, and justifies final decision.
propositions.quote: Subsection 110(6) of the Act delineates when the RAD is permitted to hold a hearing. It states that the RAD can hold a hearing when there is new evidence that raises a serious credibility issue. Further, the evidence must be central to the decision. In addition, there is a requirement that the evidence would justify a final decision allowing or rejecting the claim.

paragraphs.summary: The law permits RAD hearings only if new evidence raises serious credibility issues, is central, and justifies a final decision.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the new evidence raises serious credibility issues, is central, and justifies allowing the claim and a hearing.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argued that the evidence raises a serious credibility issue, is central to the decision, and would justify allowing the claim. For these reasons, the Appellant argues that evidence should be accepted onto the record, and the Appellant should be granted a hearing.

propositions.text: The evidence does not raise serious credibility issues, is not central or determinative, and does not justify a hearing.
propositions.quote: I find that the evidence does not raise a serious issue regarding credibility; it was already on the record. Further, for reasons that will be given, the evidence is not central nor is it determinative. At best, the evidence addresses parts of the claim, but it does not address the central issue, which is the likely level of risk for the Appellant in Pakistan. Further, it does not address whether an IFA is reasonably available in a manner that is determinative.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the evidence justifies a hearing; the court finds it does not raise serious credibility issues or address central issues.

propositions.text: The RAD will not hold a hearing.
propositions.quote: The RAD will not hold a hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD decides not to hold a hearing.

propositions.text: Gender is a ground of persecution under the Refugee Convention; domestic violence and spouse choice are recognized bases for fear of persecution.
propositions.quote: Certainly, gender is a ground of persecution in accordance with the Convention on Refugees. Further, section 1(3) of the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution notes that domestic violence is a basis for a well-founded fear of persecution as well as when women choose their spouses.

propositions.text: The central issue in this claim is credibility.
propositions.quote: That is not in issue. In this claim, the central issue is credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Gender is a recognized persecution ground; the central issue here is credibility.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD's questions were microscopic and overly detailed.
propositions.quote: In her Appeal Memorandum, the Appellant argues that the RPD's questions were microscopic.

propositions.text: The RPD's questions were detailed but relevant; guidance and interpreter were provided; Counsel did not object.
propositions.quote: I agree that, at times, they were very detailed. However, they were also about relevant issues. Further, the RPD did provide guidance on how to answer, and there was an interpreter. The Appellant was represented by Counsel, who did not object to the questions.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant claims RPD's questions were microscopic; the court finds them detailed but relevant with proper guidance and no objection.

propositions.text: Credibility is key to assessing well-founded fear of persecution; the Appellant's testimony has significant issues and is vague.
propositions.quote: The issue of credibility arises in the assessment of whether the Appellant has a well-founded fear of persecution. I find that there are significant issues with the Appellant's testimony. Overall, the Appellant's evidence was vague.

paragraphs.summary: Credibility is central; the Appellant's testimony is vague and problematic.

propositions.text: The evidence about the 2016 assault is vague but relevant to assessing future risk.
propositions.quote: The evidence about the assault on September 6, 2016 in Chauburji, Lahore is vague. This is a central issue, as the level of harm the Appellant faced in the past is a relevant consideration for forward-looking risk.

paragraphs.summary: The 2016 assault evidence is vague but relevant to assessing future risk.

propositions.text: There is insufficient credible evidence that the Appellant was attacked by husband's ex-wife's family due to her marriage; details were vague.
propositions.quote: There is insufficient credible evidence to conclude that the Appellant was attacked by her husband's ex-wife's family because of her marriage. The Appellant did not provide a description of it; rather, she provided vague answers.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified about an assault causing bleeding, neck fracture, and iron weapon, but gave no details on context or protection.
propositions.quote: She testified that three members of her husband's ex-wife's family came to her home and assaulted her. Her head was bleeding; her neck was fractured, and they had an iron. She did not provide information about what was said, whether she was alone, or how she tried to protect herself.

propositions.text: She recognized assailants from pictures.
propositions.quote: She indicated that she recognized the relatives as she had seen pictures.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds insufficient credible evidence of the 2016 attack due to vague testimony lacking detail.

propositions.text: The traumatic event could affect testimony but vagueness is not limited to it; hospital treatment and medical report issues noted.
propositions.quote: That is a traumatic event; I have considered that it could affect the Appellant's testimony. However, it is not the only area of the evidence that was vague. The RPD questioned the Appellant about why there was not a medical report on record. The Appellant testified that the hospital would not treat her without a police report. The RPD noted that it was odd that the hospital would want to have a police report before it provided treatment. The Appellant agreed.

propositions.text: The Appellant's explanation about medical report unavailability is unclear and inconsistent.
propositions.quote: The Appellant also testified that she could not get a medical record, as "they said" it was done on a humanitarian basis. She appears to be indicating that the clinic refused because they provided treatment on a humanitarian basis and that they were concerned that there would be trouble if they provided a report. It is unclear why a medical report was not available before the RPD hearing. Further, testimony regarding the steps that the Appellant took before the hearing to obtain a medical report is not clear.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes vagueness beyond trauma, finds hospital treatment and medical report explanations unclear and inconsistent.

propositions.text: The medical report from Pakistan lacks probative value and does not support the assault account.
propositions.quote: I have also considered the medical report from the clinic in Pakistan that the Appellant provided to the RAD. I do not find that it has probative value to support the Appellant's account of an assault from her husband's ex-wife's family.

propositions.text: The report is handwritten, undated, lacks injury cause, and contradicts Appellant's testimony about head injury and loss of consciousness.
propositions.quote: It is unclear why, about two years after the assault, the clinic would provide a handwritten document when they would not do so earlier without a police report. The document does not state anything about how an injury occurred; nor does it state when the injury occurred. The Appellant testified about a neck fracture, that her head was bleeding, and that the assailants had an iron. She stated that she fell down, and they thought she was dead. Further, in her Basis of Claim (BOC) form, the Appellant testified that she was hit on her head until she lost consciousness.

propositions.text: The medical report states a left foot fracture and superficial hand burn, which the Appellant partially mentioned but did not testify about head injury or burn.
propositions.quote: However, the medical report does not state that there was a head injury or a leg injury. This is particularly significant as the Appellant's evidence is that the head injury was so severe that she lost consciousness. The medical report only states that there was a left foot fracture and superficial burn on the left hand. The Appellant did not testify about a burn; however, she did write in her BOC that there were burns on her hand.

propositions.text: The report is marked 'not valid for court' and is given no weight.
propositions.quote: The report also has a statement that it is "(not valid for court)" written on. I am unable to give this report weight.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the medical report unreliable, contradictory, and gives it no weight in supporting the assault claim.

propositions.text: Significant discrepancies exist between the medical report and the Appellant's evidence about head injuries from the attack.
propositions.quote: I find that there are significant discrepancies in the medical report from the Appellant's evidence regarding the injuries from the attack.

propositions.text: Some inconsistencies like burns or fractured leg/foot are not significant, but the head injury discrepancy is significant.
propositions.quote: While some inconsistencies are not significant, such as whether or not the Appellant sustained burns or whether it was her leg or her foot that was fractured, the discrepancy with the head injury is a significant discrepancy.

propositions.text: Omission in the medical report undermines its probative value and it does not persuasively link injuries to husband's ex-wife's family.
propositions.quote: Further, the omission in the medical report significantly undermines the report's probative value. Nor does the report provide persuasive evidence that her husband's ex-wife's family attacked the Appellant; it merely states that, at some point, the Appellant had injuries.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds significant discrepancies in the medical report versus the Appellant's evidence, undermining the report's value and its link to the alleged attackers.

propositions.text: Prescriptions for Naproxen only show the Appellant had prescriptions, not how or for what injury they were given.
propositions.quote: Similarly, the prescription for Naproxen provided to the RPD simply provides evidence that the Appellant had a prescription of Naproxen.

propositions.text: These prescriptions provide limited evidence and do not describe the injury or its cause.
propositions.quote: They do not provide probative evidence about how the injury occurred. They do not describe what injury the prescription is for. This is limited evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Naproxen prescriptions provide limited evidence and do not explain the injury or its cause.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence exists to find injuries resulted from assault by husband's ex-wife's family.
propositions.quote: there is insufficient evidence to find that it was the result of an assault from the family of her husband's ex-wife.

propositions.text: Appellant's evidence about the assault is vague and corroborative evidence is insufficient to overcome weaknesses.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's evidence regarding the assault is vague, and corroborative evidence is not sufficient to address the weakness in the evidence.

propositions.text: Appellant has not shown it is more likely than not that husband's ex-wife's family assaulted her.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not demonstrated that it is more likely than not that the family of the husband's ex-wife assaulted her.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds insufficient evidence that the Appellant was assaulted by the husband's ex-wife's family and that her assault evidence is vague.

propositions.text: Appellant's testimony about threats from her family, especially one brother, is vague and unclear about who threatened her.
propositions.quote: Further, while the Appellant testified that she received threats from her family, specifically one brother, this evidence is also vague. It is not clear who in her family threatened her

propositions.text: Appellant testified about about 15 threats over a five-year period but could not specify timing or details.
propositions.quote: she received about 15 threats. It was unclear when she received the threats... she could not describe when in the marriage this five-year period occurred.

propositions.text: Appellant's description of threats is vague, e.g. brother said he would kill her.
propositions.quote: While she states that he said that her brother said he would kill her, this is a vague description of the threat.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant's evidence about family threats vague and unclear regarding timing and details.

propositions.text: Evidence about threats from husband's ex-wife is clearer but inconsistent about who threatened her.
propositions.quote: The evidence regarding the threats from her husband's ex-wife is more clear... she also testified that it was only her husband's ex-wife who had threatened her; while in the BOC, she stated that it was her husband's ex-wife's family that had threatened her.

propositions.text: Appellant lived near husband's ex-wife for years without serious harm, from 2008 to 2017.
propositions.quote: Further, the Appellant lived within plain sight of her husband's ex-wife for years and did not face serious harm. Again, she was married in 2008 and stayed in Pakistan until XXXX 2017.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds inconsistent evidence about threats from husband's ex-wife and notes Appellant lived near her without serious harm for years.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence that Appellant faced serious harm; credibility concerns mainly vagueness about threats.
propositions.quote: There is also insufficient evidence that the Appellant faced serious harm. As noted before, there are credibility concerns, mainly vagueness, with the evidence regarding threats.

propositions.text: Appellant lived openly in Pakistan; no evidence she was in hiding; family knew her location.
propositions.quote: the weight of the evidence leads to the conclusion that her family knew where she was located.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence that Appellant underwent serious harm necessary to find persecution.
propositions.quote: there is insufficient evidence that she underwent the serious harm that is necessary to find that there was persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds insufficient evidence of serious harm or persecution and notes Appellant lived openly in Pakistan.

propositions.text: Cumulative evidence insufficient to find serious harm; affidavit notes stress and anxiety mainly in Canada.
propositions.quote: there is insufficient evidence to find that the Appellant has faced serious harm... she notes that she felt this significant stress while in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds cumulative evidence insufficient to show serious harm, noting stress was mainly felt in Canada.

propositions.text: Given time lapse since 2008 marriage and living in Pakistan until 2017, past persecution evidence is relevant to future risk.
propositions.quote: Given the lapse in time since the marriage, which was in 2008, and the fact that the Appellant lived in Pakistan until 2017, I find that... evidence of past persecution is relevant in assessing the likelihood of future persecution.

propositions.text: The 2008 marriage event is too remote to support a finding of likely future persecution.
propositions.quote: The event that triggered the reaction of the agents of harm, namely, the marriage in 2008 is simply too remote to sustain a finding supporting the likelihood of future persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the 2008 marriage is too remote to support likely future persecution, making past persecution relevant to future risk.

propositions.text: Lack of credible evidence weighs against likelihood of well-founded fear of persecution.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, the lack of credible evidence weighs against the likelihood of a well-founded fear of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes lack of credible evidence weighs against a well-founded fear of persecution.

propositions.text: RPD noted discrepancies between original and copy of marriage certificates, undermining Appellant's credibility.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that the stamps on the original did not appear on the copy provided to the RPD prior to the hearing... It weighs against the Appellant's credibility.

propositions.text: Appellant's explanation that husband's ex-wife has all papers is unreasonable and inconsistent.
propositions.quote: When questioned about the difference, the Appellant testified that her husband's former wife has all the papers... However, this does not provide a reasonable explanation for how the two documents are different.

propositions.text: Court defers to RPD's advantage in observing document discrepancies over RAD.
propositions.quote: The RPD was clearly in a position of significant advantage in making this observation than is the RAD; I give deference to this finding.

paragraphs.summary: The court defers to RPD's finding that marriage certificate discrepancies undermine Appellant's credibility and finds her explanation unreasonable.

propositions.text: Appellant's evidence remains too vague to be credible despite possible stress during hearing.
propositions.quote: I find that... the evidence is still too vague to be credible. I have considered that the Appellant was in a hearing and that the process can be stressful.

propositions.text: No sufficient evidence of psychological condition impairing Appellant's testimony ability.
propositions.quote: there is not sufficient evidence regarding the Appellant's psychological condition to conclude that it presented a barrier to her ability to testify.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Appellant's evidence too vague to be credible and no evidence of psychological barriers to testimony.

propositions.text: When evidence is flawed, corroborative evidence becomes more important.
propositions.quote: When the evidence is flawed, corroborative evidence is more important.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that corroborative evidence is more important when evidence is flawed.

propositions.text: Marriage certificate only shows marriage; no letters of support before RPD.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has provided a marriage certificate; however, this simply indicates that she was married. There were no letters of support before the RPD.

propositions.text: No police report on assault was provided; prescription notes have limited probative value.
propositions.quote: The Appellant testified that the police did not provide a report regarding the assault... The prescription note provided to the RPD and the one provided to the RAD have already been discussed.

propositions.text: Other documentary evidence before RAD has limited probative value.
propositions.quote: Other documentary evidence before the RAD has very limited probative value.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds documentary evidence limited, with only a marriage certificate and no police report or strong corroboration.

propositions.text: Husband's affidavit states threat from brother-in-law with police and gangster contacts, inconsistent with Appellant's testimony.
propositions.quote: In it, he states that there is a threat from his brother-in-law, who has contact with senior police officials and gangsters. This not consistent with the Appellant's testimony...

propositions.text: Husband does not explain why Appellant lived safely despite threats; affidavit has limited probative value.
propositions.quote: The husband does not address why, if there was this level of threat, the Appellant lived there so long safely. The affidavit has limited probative value.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds husband's affidavit inconsistent with Appellant's testimony and of limited probative value.

propositions.text: Friend's affidavit states Appellant lived with her due to threat and 2016 serious incident, but does not identify assailants.
propositions.quote: The deponent states that the Appellant came to live with her after the marriage because of the threat. Further, the 2016 incident was serious, and they tried to kill her. She does not identify who "they" are.

propositions.text: Affidavit does not connect assault or injuries to husband's ex-wife's family and is geographically distant from assault location.
propositions.quote: This evidence does not provide a connection between an assault, or even injuries, with her husband's ex-wife's family... it is unclear how much the deponent would know about it given that she is in Islamabad.

propositions.text: Appellant's assault occurred in Lahore; affidavit from Islamabad has limited probative weight.
propositions.quote: According to the Appellant's testimony, the assault occurred in Lahore, Pakistan... I am unable to give this affidavit probative weight.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the friend's affidavit lacks connection to the assault and has limited probative weight due to location and detail.

propositions.text: Cumulative documentary evidence insufficient to address issues with evidence.
propositions.quote: When I weigh the evidence on a cumulative basis, I find that the documentary evidence is not sufficient to address the issues with the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes cumulative documentary evidence is insufficient to resolve evidentiary issues.

propositions.text: Appellant argues Gender Guideline applies to reavailment issue; she returned to Pakistan due to economic dependence on husband.
propositions.quote: In her Appeal Memorandum, the Appellant has argued that the Gender Guideline applies to the issue of reavailment. She states that... she returned to Pakistan because she was a housewife and economically dependent on her husband.

propositions.text: Appellant quotes transcript noting she worked as XXXX XXXX, though testimony about work was vague.
propositions.quote: In so doing, she quotes the transcript... The testimony about her work was vague.

propositions.text: Appellant has two degrees and higher education than most in Pakistan.
propositions.quote: While she has indicated that she was a housewife for years, she also has two degrees: one in XXXX XXXX from a college and one in the XXXX from a university.

propositions.text: Appellant returned relying on husband's direction that situation in Pakistan was normal; plausible given women's situation in Pakistan.
propositions.quote: she also has two degrees... Given the situation of women in Pakistan, this is plausible.

propositions.text: Reavailment is not determinative; lack of action by agents weighs against future persecution risk.
propositions.quote: Having considered all of this evidence, I do not find reavailment is a determinative issue. Rather, there was a lack of action from the agents of persecution that weigh against the likelihood that there is a future-looking risk of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues Gender Guideline applies to reavailment; court finds reavailment not determinative and lack of agent action weighs against future risk.

propositions.text: Objective evidence shows honour killings exist, more in rural areas; militants pose greatest threat, not family members named by Appellant.
propositions.quote: Certainly, there are honour killings, even if it is illegal... While Shias are targeted, the greatest threat is from the militants, and the Appellant has identified family members and her husband's ex-wife's family as the agents of persecution.

propositions.text: IRB report notes no issues with interfaith marriages between Shia and Sunni Muslims.
propositions.quote: an Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) Response to Information Request (RIR) discussed marriages with different religions and did not note any issues with marriages between Shia and Sunni Muslims.

propositions.text: Appellant lived with husband in Pakistan about eight years with little repercussions and no serious harm; credibility issues remain.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has lived with her husband in Pakistan for about eight years with little repercussions. She has not faced serious harm, and in this appeal, it is a consideration when assessing a forward-looking risk. In addition, there are credibility issues.

propositions.text: Objective evidence issues insufficient to find Appellant is a Convention refugee given her circumstances.
propositions.quote: Given her individual circumstances, I do not find that the issues outlined in the objective evidence are sufficient to find that the Appellant is a Convention refugee.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds objective evidence shows threats mainly from militants, Appellant lived safely, and issues insufficient to find refugee status.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence that Appellant is a Convention refugee.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I find that there is not sufficient evidence that the Appellant is a Convention refugee.

propositions.text: RPD overemphasized BOC discrepancies and had high expectations for precise answers.
propositions.quote: I have considered that the RPD over emphasized the discrepancies with the BOC and that, at times, its expectations for precise answers may have been too high.

propositions.text: Gender Guideline factors not relevant to RPD hearing or RAD.
propositions.quote: Further, I have considered the factors set out in section D of the Gender Guideline which address special problems at RPD hearings and find that they are not relevant for the RPD hearing or before the RAD.

propositions.text: Appellant may have been stressed but no psychological report shows barrier to testimony; RPD gave clear directions.
propositions.quote: I have considered that the Appellant may have been stressed at the hearing; however, there is not a psychological report to show any barrier to testimony, and the RPD was clear in his directions for testimony.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence on treatment of women in Pakistan considered but credible evidence of serious harm lacking.
propositions.quote: I have considered the documentary evidence regarding the treatment of women in Pakistan. However, there still has to be sufficient credible evidence of a serious possibility of serious harm, and there is not.

propositions.text: Even if not correct, Appellant has an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Islamabad.
propositions.quote: However, even if this is not correct, I find that the Appellant has an IFA in Islamabad.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds insufficient evidence of refugee status, notes RPD's overemphasis on discrepancies, and finds Appellant has an IFA in Islamabad.

propositions.text: Appellant has an IFA in Islamabad; only one city needs to be considered for IFA.
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant has an IFA in Islamabad, the capital of Pakistan... there only needs to be one IFA for the Appellant.

propositions.text: Appellant argues RPD erred by not considering both cities for IFA.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has argued that the RPD erred when it did not consider both cities; however, there only needs to be one IFA for the Appellant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Appellant has an IFA in Islamabad and rejects her argument that RPD erred by not considering both cities.

propositions.text: The test for assessing an IFA is two-pronged from Rasaratnam: no serious persecution risk and reasonable to seek refuge there.
propositions.quote: The test for assessing an IFA is two-pronged and is set out in the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Rasaratnam.20 (1) The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA. (2) Moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for him to seek refuge there.21

paragraphs.summary: The court states the two-pronged test for an IFA from Rasaratnam: no serious persecution risk and reasonable to seek refuge there.

propositions.text: Both prongs must be satisfied; burden is on appellant to prove no IFA; IFA must be realistic and not cause undue hardship.
propositions.quote: Both prongs must be satisfied to find that an appellant has an IFA. Once the issue of IFA has been raised and the potential IFAs have been identified, the burden of proof rests with an appellant to show that he/she does not have an IFA. The finding of an IFA must be based on a distinct evaluation of the region for that purpose taking into account an appellant's personal circumstances. An IFA must be a realistic and attainable option. An appellant cannot be required to encounter great physical danger or undergo undue hardship in traveling there and staying there.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains both prongs must be met, burden on appellant to disprove IFA, and IFA must be realistic without undue hardship.

propositions.text: The RPD properly raised Islamabad and Hyderabad as potential IFAs; burden shifted to appellant to show serious persecution risk in Islamabad.
propositions.quote: The RPD properly raised Islamabad and Hyderabad as locations for an IFA. The onus of proof has shifted to the Appellant. Is there a serious possibility of persecution in Islamabad?

paragraphs.summary: The court notes RPD identified Islamabad and Hyderabad as IFAs and burden shifted to appellant to show persecution risk in Islamabad.

propositions.text: Appellant stated risk to life was only reason she could not relocate; had a home in Islamabad for six years without serious harm.
propositions.quote: When asked at the hearing whether the Appellant could relocate, the Appellant stated that the only reason was a risk to her life.22 She noted that she had a call while she was in Islamabad. The family of the first wife has strong connections. The Appellant would have to show proof of identity to rent a place; this presents a risk. However, I find that the same considerations noted above regarding the likelihood of persecution apply to this analysis. Further, according to the evidence, the Appellant had a home in Islamabad for a significant period of time and did not face serious harm. The Government of Canada Citizenship and Immigration Schedule A states that the Appellant had a home in Islamabad for six years, from April 2008 until August 2014.23 While she also noted in this form that she had an address in Lahore for one year during this period as well, the evidence is that she lived in Islamabad for quite a few years. Even if she received threats there, I have addressed the threats and find that they do not amount to serious harm.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant lived in Islamabad for six years without serious harm despite some threats and risk concerns.

propositions.text: Appellant argues she would face persecution in Islamabad as a Shia Muslim and RAD must consider this ground.
propositions.quote: In her Appeal Memorandum, the Appellant has argued that she would face persecution in Islamabad as she is a Shia Muslim. She argues that the RAD has a duty to consider a ground that is evident on the face of it.

propositions.text: Court considered evidence of sectarian violence; attacks occur but not prevalent in Islamabad; appellant lived there without persecution evidence.
propositions.quote: I have considered this argument as it is evident on the record. The Appellant quotes the US Department of State report for Pakistan in 201724 and the UK Home Office report25 to show that there is sectarian violence. I have considered the documentary evidence on this issue. It shows that extremist militants have attacked Iman Bargahs and Shia Muslims. However, as noted by the quote cited by the Appellant in her Appeal Memorandum, these attacks are more prevalent in certain areas.26 This same report also states that intensity and frequency of the targeting may vary from region to region.27 As noted in the UK Home Office report quoted by the Appellant, these areas do not include Islamabad. Again, the Appellant had a home in Islamabad for years; there is insufficient evidence of any act of persecution from extremists and any act that would lead one to find that the Appellant is a person in need of protection. The UK Home office report directs decision-makers to consider if there has been past persecution and if it would be repeated.28 Further, each case must be assessed on the facts of the individual case.29 While this report is from another jurisdiction, the UK, I find that the principles apply to this case. In this individual case, the Appellant has lived in Pakistan for years without evidence of persecution from extremists; rather, the agents of harm were family members as addressed above. Further, there is insufficient evidence of a forward-looking risk.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues risk of persecution as a Shia Muslim; the court finds insufficient evidence of persecution in Islamabad and notes family, not extremists, were agents of harm.

propositions.text: Is there sufficient credible evidence of serious persecution risk in Islamabad?
propositions.quote: There is insufficient credible evidence of a serious possibility of persecution in Islamabad. Is it reasonable for the Appellant to relocate to Islamabad?

paragraphs.summary: The court finds insufficient credible evidence of serious persecution risk in Islamabad and raises the issue of reasonableness of relocation.

propositions.text: Gender Guideline C4 requires considering women's ability to travel safely and stay without undue hardship when assessing IFA reasonableness.
propositions.quote: I have considered whether the Appellant relocated and lived in Islamabad would constitute undue hardship. In so doing, I have considered the Gender Guideline. Notably, at section C4, it states that: In determining the reasonableness of a woman's recourse to an internal flight alternative (IFA), decision-makers should consider the ability of women, because of their gender, to travel safely to the IFA and to stay there without facing undue hardship. In determining the reasonableness of an IFA, the decision-makers should take into account factors including religious, economic, and cultural factors, and consider whether and how these factors affect women in the IFA.

paragraphs.summary: The court applies Gender Guideline C4 to consider if relocating to Islamabad would cause undue hardship for the appellant as a woman.

propositions.text: There is an airport in Islamabad and no evidence appellant would face undue hardship traveling there.
propositions.quote: There is an airport in Islamabad;30 there is not sufficient evidence to conclude that the Appellant would not be able to travel there without facing undue hardship.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence that traveling to Islamabad would cause undue hardship for the appellant.

propositions.text: Appellant lived in Islamabad six years, has resources, education, husband support, and work experience aiding relocation.
propositions.quote: I have considered economic factors. The Appellant lived in Islamabad for about six years. She has significant resources. The weight of the evidence leads to the conclusion that she would have the support of her husband. She is highly educated with two post-secondary degrees. She has worked in an office. She has travelled. These assets would assist her in finding employment, if she needed to do so.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant's economic and personal resources support her ability to relocate to Islamabad without undue hardship.

propositions.text: No evidence religion, language, or accommodation would hinder relocation; Shia communities and languages present in Islamabad.
propositions.quote: There is insufficient evidence that religion, language or accommodation would present a barrier in relocating. There are Shia communities throughout Pakistan with Shia Mosques and places of worship in most major cities and towns.31 Islamabad is a major city. As noted above, I have considered the treatment of the Shia Muslims in Pakistan. Further, the Appellant speaks Urdu as well as some Punjabi and English;32 Urdu is the official language of Pakistan and Punjabi and is spoken by 48% of the population.33 The Appellant has already lived in Islamabad, and there is insufficient evidence to conclude that there were issues with accommodation or that it would be an issue if she relocated there. The weight of the evidence is that these factors would not present undue hardship to relocating.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence that religion, language, or accommodation would cause undue hardship for appellant relocating to Islamabad.

propositions.text: No evidence cultural factors or gender issues would cause undue hardship for appellant relocating to Islamabad.
propositions.quote: Similarly, in this appeal, there is insufficient evidence that any cultural factor would be an issue. There is evidence regarding the treatment of women in Pakistan, but I must consider this individual in her circumstances. She has significant resources. There is insufficient evidence that she has encountered issues relating to her gender in the past that would constitute undue hardship or that she is likely to do so in the future.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence that cultural or gender factors would cause undue hardship for appellant relocating to Islamabad.

propositions.text: Appellant testified risk to life was only relocation barrier; court finds no cumulative undue hardship to relocating to Islamabad.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has testified that the only reason she could not relocate was because of the risk to life. Even on a cumulative basis, the weight of the evidence is that the factors considered, when assessing whether it is reasonable to relocate, do not present barriers to relocation. I find that the Appellant would not face undue hardship in relocating to Islamabad. Is the Appellant a Person in Need of Protection in accordance with Section 97?

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant's only relocation barrier was risk to life, but no undue hardship exists to relocating to Islamabad.

propositions.text: Higher burden to prove person in need of protection under s.97 than Convention refugee under s.96; insufficient evidence for either here.
propositions.quote: I find that there is also insufficient evidence that the Appellant is a person in need of protection. The burden of proof to establish one is a person in need of protection is higher than that for a Convention refugee. The standard to establish that one is a Convention refugee, in accordance with section 96 of the Act, is whether there is more than a mere possibility; the standard to establish that one is a person in need of protection, in accordance with section 97 of the Act, is whether, on a balance of probabilities, one is in need of protection. One must show that there is merely a risk of persecution under section 96. Section 97 stipulates that one must show that there is a danger of torture; alternatively, that there is a risk to one's life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. The level of proof required to establish a sufficient risk is higher under section 97 than it is in section 96. As there is insufficient evidence to establish that the Appellant faces more than a mere possibility of persecution in Pakistan, there is also insufficient evidence that she is a person in need of protection in Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains higher burden under s.97 than s.96 and finds insufficient evidence appellant is a person in need of protection.

propositions.text: Same considerations for IFA apply to section 97 protection assessment.
propositions.quote: In addition, I note that the same considerations for an IFA apply to section 97.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes same considerations for IFA apply to section 97 protection assessment.

propositions.text: RAD dismisses appeal and confirms RPD decision appellant is neither Convention refugee nor person in need of protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms RPD decision appellant is neither Convention refugee nor person in need of protection.
